summary: Defines a way to remotely trigger MPLS pings on label switched paths. A Proxy Ping Request can be sent to any router along a path, which then runs the test. This reduces message counts and processing and enables checks that the sender cannot do directly.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of knocking on every door yourself, you ask a helper partway down the street to do the knocking and report back.

questions: how does proxy lsp ping work
what udp port does mpls ping use
subtitle: How one router can ask another router on an MPLS path to run a ping test on its behalf.

tldr.problem: Pinging a large point-to-multipoint MPLS tree from the root makes many routers process and answer the request, and a leaf has no way to trace back toward the root.
tldr.mechanism: An initiator sends a Proxy Ping Request to a router on the path. That Proxy LSR checks that it is allowed to act, then either sends the MPLS Echo Request itself with a small TTL or replies with neighbor and mapping information.
tldr.outcome: Tests can start from any router on the path and stay small, but the facility is meant only for use inside one operator's network and under its authority.

today: RFC 7555 is a Proposed Standard from June 2015. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Proxy Ping Is Needed
sections.content:
The RFC 4379 MPLS ping sends an MPLS Echo Request down a Label Switched Path (LSP). On a Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP) tree the request is replicated at every branch, so routers that are not on the path being tested still process it and send replies. The root can be overwhelmed by the number of replies.

The second motivation is tracing from a leaf toward the root. This is the natural direction for LDP-based P2MP and Multipoint-to-Multipoint (MP2MP) LSPs (RFC 6388), where the root may know only its adjacent downstream nodes, while a leaf knows its upstream neighbor. The leaf asks that neighbor to ping across the final link, learns the neighbor's own upstream neighbor, and repeats until the fault is found or the root is reached. The TTL needs to be at most 2 each time, so only a few nodes see each request.

The procedures apply to all LSP Ping FEC types where the echo messages are IP encapsulated and the reply can go out of band over IP. Testing a stack of more than one FEC, choosing the label, or adding labels to the stack is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Shouting down a huge tunnel makes everyone shout back. It is better to ask a friend near the spot you care about to check just that bit.

sections.title: Roles and Overview
sections.content:
The document adds two LSP Ping messages, the MPLS Proxy Ping Request and the MPLS Proxy Ping Reply. A remote ping involves at least three routers, and in some cases none of them is the ingress or an egress of the LSP. The RFC names four roles:

  • Initiator: sends the Proxy Ping Request.
  • Proxy LSR: the destination of that request, and the potential sender of the MPLS Echo Request.
  • Receivers: the routers that receive the MPLS Echo Request.
  • Responder: a receiver that answers.

Because the Proxy LSR sends the echo on behalf of the initiator, it keeps no state to handle the answers. Responders send their replies to the initiator or to another router set up to handle them.

The request tells the Proxy LSR to do one of two things: send an MPLS Echo Request in-band on the LSP, or reply with proxy information such as neighbor addresses or downstream maps. The initiator uses that information to build its next request.
sections.plainLanguage: There is the person asking, the helper who goes and checks, and whoever answers the helper's knock. The helper does not need to remember anything afterwards.

sections.title: What the Initiator Sends
sections.content:
The request MUST contain a Target FEC Stack describing what is being tested, and the topmost FEC is used by the Proxy LSR to find the label stack for the echo. It MUST also contain a Proxy Echo Parameters TLV. In that TLV the initiator sets the address type (IPv4 or IPv6) and a destination address, which MUST come from 127/8 for IPv4 or ::ffff:7f00:0/104 for IPv6. It also supplies the reply mode, global flags, source UDP port and the TTL for the outgoing label stack.

Other optional pieces include Next Hop sub-TLVs to limit where the echo goes, and downstream mapping TLVs. To test an LSP's MTU, the initiator can set the MPLS Payload Size so the Proxy LSR pads the echo with a Pad TLV; in that case the request MUST NOT carry a Pad TLV itself, and the IP DF bit MUST be set.

The request travels in a UDP packet to destination port 3503 with the IP TTL set to 255. It is sent to the Proxy LSR using ordinary IP forwarding.
sections.plainLanguage: The asker writes a note saying what path to test, how far to go and how to answer, and hands it to the helper.

sections.title: What the Proxy LSR Does
sections.content:
The Proxy LSR first checks that the message is well formed and that it understands the TLVs not marked "Ignore". Problems lead to the return codes "Malformed echo request received" or "TLV not understood". It then checks that it has a label mapping for the FEC and that the initiator is authorized. A Proxy LSR MUST be able to filter initiator addresses. A request that arrives through IP or label TTL expiry, or addressed to a loopback address, MUST be treated as unauthorized. The reply MAY then carry Return Code 16, "Proxy Ping not authorized".

The TTL in the parameters must be in the range 1 to 255; otherwise the Return Code is 17, "Proxy Ping parameters need to be modified".

If the initiator set a flag asking for FEC neighbor addresses or for a downstream map, the Proxy LSR sends no echo and instead returns the information in a Proxy Ping Reply. Otherwise it builds an MPLS Echo Request, copying the global flags, reply mode, sender's handle and sequence number, and sends it on each chosen next hop. The echo source address is the Reply-to Address if present, otherwise the source of the request. Any extra labels pushed get TTL 255 so the requester cannot control tunnels unrelated to the FEC.

When the Proxy LSR is itself an egress or a bud node, it generally replies with Return Code 3, "Replying router is an egress for the FEC at stack-depth". New Return Code 19 means the router has a mapping for the topmost FEC.

A Proxy LSR that does not understand LSP Ping at all MUST drop the message and MUST NOT send anything back to the initiator.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper first checks that the note looks right and that the person asking is allowed to ask. Only then does the helper go knock, or write back what it knows.

sections.title: Messages and TLV Formats
sections.content:
The packet format is that of RFC 4379, with two new message types: 3 for the Proxy Ping Request and 4 for the Proxy Ping Reply. The RFC also defines four new TLVs: Proxy Echo Parameters (23), Reply-to Address (24), Upstream Neighbor Address (25) and Downstream Neighbor Address (26).

The Proxy Echo Parameters TLV has a length of 12 + K + S, where K is the destination address length and S the total length of the sub-TLVs. It is used either to control how an echo is built or to query the Proxy LSR about the topmost FEC, but not both. Its Proxy Flags are:

  • 0x0001 request for FEC neighbor address info
  • 0x0002 request for Downstream Mapping
  • 0x0004 request for Downstream Detailed Mapping
  • 0x0008 explicit DSCP request

The first three cancel sending an echo, and the two mapping flags cannot both be set. The only sub-TLV is Next Hop (type 1), which names a next hop address and interface the echo should go toward. The Upstream and Downstream Neighbor Address TLVs carry a neighbor address and the local address used in the protocol adjacency that exchanged the label for the FEC.
sections.plainLanguage: The note has a fixed form with boxes to fill in: where to send, how far, and whether you want an answer about neighbors instead of a test.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mechanism is intended for use within a service provider network and only under the authority of that administration. If the network carries Internet traffic or allows IP access from other administrations, Proxy Ping messages SHOULD be discarded where such packets enter, by filtering on source address or on the MPLS ping UDP port.

A Proxy LSR SHOULD validate requests against a set of valid source addresses, and an implementation MUST provide that filtering. A request that reaches the router by TTL expiry MUST NOT be acted on, and neither MUST one whose source address is not IP reachable by the Proxy LSR. Because a request can only name a FEC, only valid MPLS Echo Request messages can be created, and the RFC states that no label-spoofing attacks are possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Only people inside the building are allowed to ask the helper. Requests from outside get thrown away.

sections.title: IANA Assignments and Registries
sections.content:
IANA assigned message types 3 and 4, TLV types 23 to 26, and Return Codes 16 (Proxy Ping not authorized), 17 (Proxy Ping parameters need to be modified), 18 (MPLS Echo Request could not be sent) and 19 (Replying router has FEC mapping for topmost FEC).

Three new registries were created: Proxy Echo Parameters Sub-TLVs (0 is Reserved, 1 is Next Hop), Proxy Flags (bits 0 to 3 assigned, 4 to 15 unassigned, Standards Action) and the Next Hop Address Type Registry (types 1 to 4 from RFC 4379, 5 Reserved, 6 and 7 for protocol adjacency, 8 to 255 unassigned). The document also marks types 6 and 7 as Reserved in the Downstream Address Mapping Registry defined by RFC 6426.
sections.plainLanguage: The numbers used in the messages were put in an official list so nobody picks the same number for a different meaning.

messages.label: MPLS Proxy Ping Request
messages.note: Sent by IP to UDP port 3503.

messages.label: MPLS Echo Reply
messages.note: Sent back to the initiator or a router set up to handle it.

fields.name: Reply Mode
fields.desc: Reply mode to use in the MPLS Echo Request.

fields.name: Proxy Flags
fields.desc: Requests actions at the Proxy LSR.

fields.name: TTL
fields.desc: TTL for the topmost FEC label, 1 to 255.

fields.name: Rqst'd DSCP
fields.desc: Valid only if the Explicit DSCP flag is set.

fields.name: Source UDP Port
fields.desc: Source port for the MPLS Echo Request.

fields.name: Global Flags
fields.desc: Global flags for the MPLS Echo Request.

items.label: FEC Neighbor Address info
items.desc: Return upstream and downstream neighbor addresses; cancels the echo.

items.label: Downstream Mapping
items.desc: Return a Downstream Mapping TLV; cancels the echo.

items.label: Downstream Detailed Mapping
items.desc: Return a Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV; cancels the echo.

items.label: Explicit DSCP Request
items.desc: Use the supplied DSCP byte in the echo.
